cards.front: Why is the inside of a resting neurone negative compared with the outside?
cards.back: The **sodium–potassium pump** uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in, and the membrane is partially permeable: K⁺ leaks out through open channels far more easily than Na⁺ leaks in.
cards.hint: Consider the energy cost of the pump and which ion leaks through the membrane more easily.

cards.front: What sequence of events takes the membrane from threshold to a full action potential?
cards.back: At about $-55\,\mathrm{mV}$, many **voltage-gated sodium channels** open and Na⁺ enters. This depolarises the membrane further, opening more channels by positive feedback, so the potential rises rapidly to about $+40\,\mathrm{mV}$.
cards.hint: Start from the moment the first few sodium channels open after the stimulus.

cards.front: What happens to the size of an action potential when the stimulus is made stronger?
cards.back: The size stays the same. This is the **all-or-nothing principle**: a stronger stimulus produces more impulses per second, not larger ones.
cards.hint: Compare what changes in the stimulus with what changes in each impulse.

cards.back: The **membrane potential** is the difference in electrical potential between the inside and outside of a cell, measured in millivolts ($\mathrm{mV}$).

cards.front: How is threshold defined in a neurone?
cards.back: **Threshold** is the membrane potential, about $-55\,\mathrm{mV}$, at which enough voltage-gated sodium channels open to trigger an action potential.

cards.front: What are the four phases of an action potential, in order?
cards.back: **Depolarisation**, then **repolarisation**, then **hyperpolarisation**, then recovery, when the pump and leak channels restore the resting potential and ion balance.
cards.hint: Start from the moment sodium channels open.

cards.front: Why does the potential dip below the resting potential at the end of an action potential?
cards.back: Potassium channels close slowly after repolarisation. Extra K⁺ ions leave the cell, so the inside becomes more negative than the resting potential, which is **hyperpolarisation**.
cards.hint: Think about how quickly each type of channel closes.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say the sodium–potassium pump causes repolarisation?
cards.back: Repolarisation is caused by K⁺ leaving through open channels. The pump does not do this; it works afterwards to restore the ion balance.
cards.hint: Which ion movement brings the potential back towards its resting value?

cards.front: A recording shows a resting potential of $-70\,\mathrm{mV}$ and a peak of $+40\,\mathrm{mV}$. What is the change in membrane potential during depolarisation?
cards.hint: Use the formula for a change: final value minus initial value.

cards.front: Why can an action potential only travel forwards along an axon?
cards.back: The membrane behind the impulse is in its **refractory period**, so its sodium channels cannot open. It cannot depolarise, so the impulse spreads only into membrane that is ready to respond.
cards.hint: Think about what the membrane just behind the impulse is able to do straight afterwards.

cards.back: **Saltatory conduction** is the jumping of an impulse from one node of Ranvier to the next along a myelinated axon.
cards.hint: Think about where the axon membrane is exposed in a myelinated axon.

cards.front: Why are impulses faster along a myelinated axon than an unmyelinated one?
cards.back: Myelin insulates the membrane, so action potentials form only at the nodes of Ranvier. Local currents carry depolarisation from node to node, which is faster than depolarising the whole membrane.
cards.hint: Compare where action potentials form in each type of axon.

cards.front: Which other factors change how fast an impulse travels, and why?
cards.back: A wider axon offers less resistance to local currents, so impulses travel faster. A higher temperature speeds up diffusion and channel opening, until proteins begin to denature.
cards.hint: Think about resistance to local currents, and about what heat does to proteins.
